KEY MESSAGE 1... 
With one round of showers and storms exiting stage right into 
PA, all attention turns back to the west as a new complex has 
developed across northern Illinois into southwestern Lower 
Michigan. This area of shower and storm activity is being fueled
by the warm air advection entering the region with the front 
lifting back north after the first round of activity. In 
addition, a potent low level jet with 30 to 35 kt of 925 mb flow
will provide extra support for storm activity. The main 
question with this complex is: Where is it going? The activity 
south of Chicago is trying to follow the instability gradient 
and should allow for this activity to dive more southeast into 
Indiana and potentially southwest Ohio. This cluster should 
remain out of the forecast area. The more concerning portion of 
the complex are the storms over southwestern Lower Michigan. 
Storms are presently moving in a northeasterly direction. 
Meanwhile, storms closer to Grand Rapids are more tied to a 
boundary that arcs southeast into northern Ohio. Over the next 
couple of hours, expect these storms to congeal over southern 
Michigan. If they can organize a touch and form a cold pool, 
these storms do have the potential to move southeast and push 
toward the forecast area later this morning. If these storms 
just remain forced by the low level jet and end up staying tied
to the surface boundary, then it is possible that this batch 
could miss much of the area to the north or at least move
over/along Lake Erie. There is some elevated instability to 
work with ahead of this complex and precipitable water values 
around 1.75" depict that rain could have some efficiency. Storms
should also quickly perk up with daytime heating as these will 
move through the region as the sun rises and activity could 
become concerning quickly after daybreak once the low level 
inversion mixes out. 

This morning round of showers and thunderstorms will then dictate 
how the rest of the day will evolve. If the activity goes through 
most of the forecast area, then the front will be south of the area 
and new activity would not be favored during the daytime hours. If 
the morning activity stays north or just stays near Lake Erie, then 
most of the forecast area will remain south of the front in a 
conditionally unstable airmass with warm advection across the area. 
This would then allow for scattered shower and storm activity to 
develop over the area during the afternoon and evening hours. Storms 
would then have the potential for strong to damaging wind gusts and 
heavy rain that could bring localized flooding. These storms could 
persist into tonight.

For tonight, all attention returns back to Wisconsin and Illinois 
for the development of a new complex of showers and thunderstorms 
that will move southeast along the front. Again, the location of the 
front will be very important on where this complex will go - Either 
into our area or to the southwest. If there is already activity in 
our area this afternoon and evening, then this complex will stay 
southwest but there will already be activity overhead to contend 
with. If the area is dry, then there is a greater chance of this 
complex reaching the forecast area. The average solution suggests 
that at least the southwest half of the forecast area (Roughly along 
and southwest of a line from Bowling Green to Canton) should get 
some activity tonight. 

For Tuesday, another southeastward diving MCS is expected to develop 
west of the forecast area during the morning hours. This complex 
should reach the area during the afternoon hours, favoring the 
southwest portion of the forecast area, roughly along and southwest 
of a Findlay to Millersburg line. Given that this complex will move 
through peak heating hours with maximum instability, there should be 
a severe wind threat that will materialize with this complex. 
Meanwhile, forecast soundings ahead of this complex show 
precipitable water values creeping back up to 1.80" showing that 
this complex will bring more heavy rain to the area. With this 
potentially being the third or fourth round of rain in 48 hours,
the risk for flash flooding will increase. 

For Tuesday night into Wednesday, the frontal boundary that has 
sustained these multiple rounds of storms should be south of the 
forecast area, allowing for any new development to favor areas to 
the southwest. There is some potential for the boundary to be close 
to our southwest counties and some scattered rain activity will be 
possible through Wednesday but the main severe and heavy rain 
threats should be out of the area. If the front does have trouble 
clearing the area with all of the uncertainty with the previous
rounds of storms, then there could be more severe weather 
potential or heavy rain/flash flooding potential on Wednesday, 
which explains why some portions of northern Ohio remain in Day 
3 SPC Severe and WPC Excessive Rainfall Marginal Risks.
